title: Purpose of the CPU
starter: A chef can keep three ingredients on the worktop, twenty in the cupboard and anything else at the shop. Which is like cache, which is like RAM and which is like secondary storage? Why does the worktop make cooking faster?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Purpose of the CPU
facts: The CPU (central processing unit) processes data and instructions.
It does this by carrying out the fetch-decode-execute cycle, over and over.
It is sometimes called the brain of the computer.
stations.challenge: Write, in your own words, the purpose of a CPU.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The CPU (central processing unit) processes data and instructions.
Also credit: It does this by carrying out the fetch-decode-execute cycle, over and over.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the CPU?
questions.a: To process data and instructions by fetching, decoding and executing them

stations.name: Stage 1: Fetch
facts: The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction.
The address is copied to the MAR, and the instruction is fetched from RAM into the MDR.
The PC is incremented, so it points to the next instruction.
stations.challenge: Describe what happens to the program counter during the fetch stage.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction.
Also credit: The address is copied to the MAR, and the instruction is fetched from RAM into the MDR.

questions.q: During the fetch stage, what happens to the program counter?
questions.a: It is incremented to point to the next instruction

questions.q: Where is the instruction fetched from?

stations.name: Stage 2: Decode
facts: The instruction is now inside the CPU.
The control unit (CU) decodes it: it works out what the instruction means and what needs to be done.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The instruction is now inside the CPU.
Also credit: The control unit (CU) decodes it: it works out what the instruction means and what needs to be done.

questions.q: What does 'decode' mean in the fetch-decode-execute cycle?
questions.a: Working out what the instruction means and what needs to be done

stations.name: Stage 3: Execute
facts: The instruction is carried out. Depending on the instruction, the CPU may:
fetch data from memory to use in a calculation, done by the ALU;
jump to another instruction, or write data from the accumulator back to RAM.
stations.challenge: Give two different things that might happen during the execute stage.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The instruction is carried out. Depending on the instruction, the CPU may:
Also credit: fetch data from memory to use in a calculation, done by the ALU;

questions.q: Where are the results of calculations stored?
After the execute stage, what happens next?
questions.a: The cycle starts again with the next fetch

stations.name: The registers
facts: Registers are tiny, very fast memory locations inside the CPU.
PC: address of the next instruction. MAR: address to fetch from or write to.
MDR: data fetched or to be written. ACC: results of calculations.
stations.challenge: Complete the registers table on your worksheet.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Registers are tiny, very fast memory locations inside the CPU.
Also credit: PC: address of the next instruction. MAR: address to fetch from or write to.

questions.q: Match each register to its purpose.
questions.a: Program counter (PC) → Holds the address of the next instruction; Memory address register (MAR) → Holds the address where data is to be stored or fetched; Memory data register (MDR) → Holds data fetched from, or to be written to, main memory; Accumulator (ACC) → Holds the results of calculations

stations.name: Other CPU components
facts: ALU (arithmetic logic unit): performs calculations and logical decisions.
CU (control unit): decodes instructions and sends signals to control how data moves.
Cache: fast memory for frequently used instructions and data.
stations.challenge: How does the cache stop the CPU having to wait for RAM?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: ALU (arithmetic logic unit): performs calculations and logical decisions.
Also credit: CU (control unit): decodes instructions and sends signals to control how data moves.

questions.q: Match each component to what it does.
questions.a: ALU → Performs calculations and logical decisions; Control unit → Decodes instructions and controls how data moves around the CPU; Cache → Fast memory for frequently used instructions and data

questions.q: Why is cache faster to use than RAM?
questions.a: It is inside the CPU, very close to where the processing happens

final.name: Final challenge: the cycle

questions.q: Put the steps of the fetch-decode-execute cycle in order.
questions.a: The PC holds the address of the next instruction → The address is copied into the MAR → The instruction is fetched from RAM into the MDR → The PC is incremented to point to the next instruction → The control unit decodes the instruction → The instruction is executed

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe what the CPU does while a program is running.
points: The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Name two registers found in a CPU and state what each one holds.
points: The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction.
Registers are tiny, very fast memory locations inside the CPU.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: A computer's cache is full. Explain the effect this has on the CPU.
points: The CPU (central processing unit) processes data and instructions.
It does this by carrying out the fetch-decode-execute cycle, over and over.
It is sometimes called the brain of the computer.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
